text: gs is the GlideSystem global object, available automatically in every server-side script you write — Business Rules, Script Includes, Scheduled Jobs, background scripts. You've already used it for simple things like gs.nowDateTime. This lesson covers its logging methods: the tool you reach for when the Script Debugger from last lesson can't attach.

gs.info, gs.warn, and gs.error write a message at increasing severity, and both take an optional source string so you can find your own lines later when the log is full of everything else. The older gs.log is equivalent to info-level logging and still shows up constantly in legacy scripts, but gs.info is the modern, preferred form.

Here's the entire mechanism: every one of these calls writes a row into the syslog table — the same System Log you already queried with GlideRecord back in Course 3. gs.info isn't a special debugging-only channel. It's a convenient way to insert a record into a table you already know how to read, filter, and sort — nothing more magical than that.

The Script Debugger only works for synchronous execution you trigger while attached. The moment a script is async — a Business Rule queued to run later — you can't pause it. The practical fix: sprinkle gs.info calls at key points, like right after the rule fires and right after reading old and new priority, then run it.

Afterward, filter the System Log by the source string you passed as the second argument, and by the time window the transaction actually ran in. Reading that filtered list back tells you exactly which lines executed and what each variable held at each point — the same information a breakpoint would have shown you live, just captured after the fact instead.

gs.info plus the System Log is the practical workaround for exactly the cases the Script Debugger can't reach. Next lesson moves to the browser itself: DevTools, for debugging real client-side JavaScript running in the user's own browser.
